question: How does sugar become a cheap, industrial food in a century that ends slavery — and who works the cane once the slaves are freed?
summary: In the nineteenth century sugar's price falls, its volume multiplies and its production is rebuilt around machines. Beet sugar appears under Napoleon's blockade, then returns for good in Germany and across Western Europe; steam mills, the vacuum pan and the centrifuge turn Cuba and Louisiana into industrial cane lands; steamships and the Suez Canal cut freight; and British consumption rises from about 18 lb a head in 1810 to about 91 lb on the eve of 1914 ([[c1]], [[ec4]], [[te1]], [[te4]], [[te5]], [[te7]], [[ec13]]).

The same century ends slavery in the sugar colonies — in 1807 and 1808 the trade, in 1833 British slavery, in 1848 French, in 1886 Cuban, in 1888 Brazilian — but not forced labour ([[o1]], [[o2]], [[o6]], [[o7]]). Planters in Mauritius, British Guiana, Natal, Queensland, Hawaii and Cuba bring in indentured workers from India, China, Japan and the Pacific islands, some of them shipped by something close to kidnapping ([[x1]], [[x2]], [[ec10]], [[x4]], [[x5]]). Former slaves, where they can, leave the plantations altogether ([[l1]]).

Cheap sugar is also political. It is the centre of Britain's free-trade decision of 1846, the American planters' overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy and the 1898 war over Cuba ([[o5]], [[c4]], [[c5]]). And it is a new diet: jam, chocolate, soft drinks and canned fruit make sugar the food of the working class, while the first health reformers begin to warn against it ([[l4]], [[e1]], [[ec17]], [[e3]], [[t2]]).

themes.title: The industrial cane and beet factory
text: Beet sugar grows from Napoleon's bounty to Germany's million tons; the vacuum pan, steam mill and centrifuge turn cane-sugar making from a ten-day process into one of about a day; refiners consolidate into fewer, bigger firms.

themes.title: Abolition without the end of unfree labour
text: After emancipation planters turn to indentured Indians and Chinese, Melanesians and Japanese, in numbers that run to hundreds of thousands to Cuba and over a million to the Indian-labour colonies. Slave imports to Cuba continue for decades after British abolition.

themes.title: New sugar frontiers: Cuba, Louisiana, Hawaii, Natal, Queensland
text: Cuba grows from 19,000 tons to 446,000 in fifty years, Louisiana is destroyed by the Civil War and rebuilt in a decade, and Hawaii grows from 4 tons in 1836 to 13,000 in 1876. In Natal and Queensland sugar fixes racial and colonial patterns that last.

themes.title: Sugar and politics: free trade and empire
text: Britain's sugar duties and Palmerston's wry account of refining slave-grown sugar; the American tariff fights; the Hawaiian coup; the sugar-trust and Cuba in 1898.

themes.title: A food for the many
text: Prices fall 30 per cent in the 1840s and again after; sugar goes into jam, chocolate, canned fruit and fizzy drinks; working-class British diets turn to sugared tea, jam and bread; American intake goes from about 8 lb to 80 lb a year.

turning_points.text: Napoleon's blockade and the British blockade choke off Europe's cane sugar and prompt a beet-sugar industry.
Britain and the United States prohibit the slave trade, yet Africans keep being landed in Cuba.
British emancipation, with a four- to six-year 'apprenticeship'.
The centrifuge and vacuum pan cut the time to crystallise sugar from days to hours.
Britain abolishes its sugar duties: free-trade sugar floods in and the West Indian privileges end.
The American Civil War wrecks Louisiana's sugar industry.
Cuba and Brazil abolish slavery, the last in the Americas.
The overthrow of the Hawaiian monarchy and the Spanish-American War bring Hawaii and Cuba under US influence.

how_to_read: The folio is the largest in the Sugar series; the *Economy* lane carries the volume (more than a dozen entries) and the *Technology* lane the machines. *Exchange* and *Lives* are where the people appear (indentured workers, former slaves, Hawaiians); *Order* has the laws.
Several entries flag source disagreements, among them the date of British annexation of Zululand and the Hawaiian treaty year. They are labelled in each note.

sources.intro: The nineteenth century is the folio's best-documented stretch, but the folio draws on only a few books, so its coverage follows theirs: the Atlantic and the Anglo-American world are strong; Java, India, the Philippines and Brazil are thin.
main: Walvin, *Sugar: The World Corrupted* (about forty-five entries).
Smith, *Sugar: A Global History*, for the American, Hawaiian and imperial entries (about twenty-five).
Mazumdar for the Chinese and the Asian side (about twenty-two), Mintz for diet.
contested: The year of British annexation of Zululand: 1887 (Smith) or 1897 (Walvin) ([[w3]]); Natal labour entry ([[ec10]]).
Walvin's reading of Gandhi's radicalisation by sugar ([[l3]]) is an interpretation, not a source.
gaps: Java's Cultivation System (from 1830), Brazil, India, the Philippines and Taiwan are thin; Deerr, Eltis and a specialist for Mauritius and Natal would help.
No primary documents for the beet industry or the sugar trust; they are cited through Walvin and Smith.
